DOCUMENT:
Budget Justification: Extended Opening Hours at Five Branch Libraries, 2027-28
Library Services, Westmoor Borough Council, September 2026

1. Request
Library Services requests a growth bid of £174,000 in the 2027-28 revenue budget to extend opening hours at five branch libraries (Ashgrove, Fenwick, Holt Lane, Kingsmead and Millbrook) by ten hours a week each, from 38 to 48 hours.

2. Rationale
The five branches currently close at 5 pm on weekdays and do not open on Sundays. Residents' surveys have repeatedly identified opening hours as the main barrier to library use among working-age adults: in the 2025 Residents' Survey, 44% of non-users aged 25-54 said the library "is never open when I can go". The Council Plan commits to increasing library use among working-age residents and to supporting adult learning and job-seeking.

Each branch would add late opening until 8 pm on Tuesdays and Thursdays (six additional hours) and Sunday opening from 11 am to 3 pm (four additional hours).

3. Evidence from the Ashgrove pilot
From October 2025 to March 2026, Ashgrove trialled exactly this pattern, funded from one-off underspends.

Table 1. Ashgrove pilot: average visits per opening hour, October 2025 to March 2026
Time slot | Visits per hour
Weekday 9 am - 12 pm | 46
Weekday 12 pm - 5 pm | 58
Tuesday and Thursday 5 pm - 8 pm (new) | 21
Saturday 9 am - 1 pm | 64
Sunday 11 am - 3 pm (new) | 52

Over the pilot, Ashgrove recorded 1,140 new library memberships, compared with 690 in the same months a year earlier. Sunday sessions were particularly popular with families, and a weekly job club in the Thursday evening slot was fully booked from its third week.

Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level, which shows that there is strong latent demand for evening opening and that the new hours will be well used across all five branches.

4. Costs
Additional hours need two staff on duty at all times, in line with the Council's lone-working policy. Staffing is calculated on 50 weeks a year, allowing for bank holiday closures.

Table 2. Cost of extended hours, five branches
Item | Basis | Cost
Staffing | 10 hours x 2 staff x 50 weeks x 5 branches = 5,000 hours at £24.80 per hour (including on-costs) | £124,000
Utilities and caretaking | £6,500 per branch | £32,500
Self-service kiosk upgrades (maintenance contract) | 5 branches | £7,500
Total | | £174,000

The staffing rate is the mid-point of the Library Assistant grade plus 28% on-costs and an enhancement for Sunday working. Utilities and caretaking costs are based on the actual additional costs recorded at Ashgrove during the pilot, scaled to a full year.

5. Value for money
At current visit rates, the extra hours across the five branches would generate roughly 84,000 additional visits a year, at a cost of around £2 per visit. This compares favourably with the borough's average cost per library visit of £3.40.

6. Alternatives considered
We considered opening the branches with self-service access only in the extra hours, as some authorities have done. This would cut staffing costs by around two-thirds, but the Council's insurers have advised that unstaffed opening would require building alterations and CCTV at an estimated £60,000 per branch, and it would not support the job club and family activities that drove much of the pilot's success.

7. Risks
Recruitment. We expect to fill most additional hours from existing part-time staff who have asked for more hours, as happened during the pilot.
Demand at other branches. Ashgrove is our busiest branch, and demand at the other four may be lower. We will review usage after six months.

8. Conclusion
The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand for evening and Sunday opening, with new memberships up by two-thirds and evening use close to daytime levels. We ask Members to approve a growth bid of £174,000 to extend this successful model to all five branches from April 2027.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "Total | | £174,000" -- The cost lines sum to £124,000 + £32,500 + £7,500 = £164,000, not £174,000. The growth bid is overstated by £10,000.
2. [inconsistency] at: "The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand" -- Section 3 states the Ashgrove pilot ran from October 2025 to March 2026, i.e. six months; the conclusion calls it a twelve-month pilot.
3. [misread_evidence] at: "Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level" -- Table 1 shows 21 visits per hour in the new weekday evening slot versus 46 and 58 in weekday daytime slots, i.e. less than half the daytime level. The text misstates the table, and the claim of strong evening demand rests on it.

REVIEW:
The bid asks for £174,000 a year to open five branch libraries ten more hours a week: Tuesday and Thursday evenings to 8 pm, and Sundays 11 am to 3 pm. It rests on three things:
- a pilot of that exact pattern at Ashgrove;
- a bottom-up costing;
- a rejected self-service alternative.

Measuring demand before asking for money is a real strength, and some of the pilot evidence is good. But the total doesn't add up to the amount requested, and the evening finding is the opposite of how the text describes it. Several other claims go beyond what the figures show.

## 1. The costs sum to £164,000, not £174,000

| Item | Cost |
|---|---|
| Staffing (5,000 hours × £24.80) | £124,000 ✓ |
| Utilities and caretaking (5 × £6,500) | £32,500 ✓ |
| Kiosk maintenance contract | £7,500 |
| **Sum of lines** | **£164,000** |
| Stated total | £174,000 |

Each line is correct, but the total is £10,000 too high. Either a line is missing or the total is wrong. That must be fixed before the bid goes to Members, because the request figure appears in §1, §8 and the cost-per-visit calculation.

## 2. Evening demand is well below daytime, not close to it

| Slot | Visits per hour |
|---|---|
| Weekday daytime, weighted average (3 h at 46, 5 h at 58) | 53.5 |
| **Tue/Thu evening (new)** | **21** |
| **Sunday (new)** | **52** |

- Evening use is about **39% of weekday daytime use**. The claim "close to daytime levels" (in §3, §8 and your description) is wrong. It looks as though the Sunday result has been attributed to evenings.
- **Sunday is the strong result.** At 52 visits an hour it is effectively level with weekday daytime, and this should be stated without hedging.

The difference matters for value for money. Staffing cost per visit for each new slot works out as follows (utilities excluded, because the paper doesn't split them by slot):

| Slot | Staff hours | Staff cost | Visits a year (5 branches) | Staff cost per visit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evenings | 3,000 | £74,400 | 31,500 | **£2.36** |
| Sundays | 2,000 | £49,600 | 52,000 | **£0.95** |

Evenings cost about two and a half times as much per visit as Sundays. Members could reasonably ask about a Sunday-only option, or Sunday plus one evening, especially if the other branches are quieter.

## 3. The demand evidence is weaker than presented

**Ashgrove is the busiest branch, but its rates are applied to all five.** The 84,000 visits figure is Ashgrove's rate for the new slots (about 16,700 a year) multiplied by five. §7 then says "demand at the other four may be lower." Both can't stand. Present 84,000 as an Ashgrove-based upper estimate, or estimate each branch from its own current visit rates.

**Visits in new hours aren't necessarily additional visits.** Some evening and Sunday visitors would otherwise have come on Saturday or a weekday. What matters is whether Ashgrove's *total* visits rose against the previous year. That figure should be available but isn't given.

**The pilot was six months, not twelve.** §3 says October 2025 to March 2026, while §8 calls it "the twelve-month Ashgrove pilot." It ran entirely in autumn and winter, so summer evening and Sunday demand is untested and could go either way.

**The membership rise is real but unattributed.**
- 1,140 against 690 is +65%, so "about two-thirds" is correct.
- It's a comparison with the previous year at one branch, with nothing to compare against. We don't know how many new members joined during the new hours, or whether there was other promotion.
- The job club being fully booked is good, specific evidence, but for one weekly session.
- §6's claim that the job club and family activities "drove much of the pilot's success" isn't measured anywhere in the paper.

**£2 per visit against £3.40 isn't like for like.** The £2 is the marginal cost of extra hours. The £3.40 borough average includes buildings, stock and management. A marginal cost will almost always look favourable against a full average cost. Compare the marginal cost per visit with that of other service options instead.

## 4. The self-service comparison is incomplete

Your description says self-service "would cost more once building works are included." The paper doesn't say that, and the figures it gives don't support it beyond the short term.
- **Saving:** about two-thirds of £124,000 in staffing, roughly £83,000 a year.
- **Cost:** £60,000 × 5 = £300,000 one-off building works (an insurer's estimate).
- **Payback:** about 3.6 years. After that, self-service is cheaper every year.

The paper's real objection is that self-service wouldn't support the job club or family activities, which is a legitimate service argument. A fair comparison would set out that trade-off over several years. It should also consider a hybrid, for example staffed Sundays and self-service evenings, or the reverse.

## 5. Smaller points on the costing

- **The Sunday enhancement:** the £24.80 rate includes "an enhancement for Sunday working." If it applies to all 5,000 hours, the 3,000 evening hours are overcosted. If it's averaged, say so.
- **The kiosk maintenance contract** (£7,500) needs a sentence explaining why a staffed extension requires it.
- **Utilities scaled from winter.** Utilities are scaled from a winter-only pilot, when heating and lighting costs are highest, so the full-year figure is probably on the high side. That makes it a conservative assumption, which is in the bid's favour.
- **The six-month review** in §7 has no decision rule attached. Say what usage level would lead to reducing or withdrawing hours at a branch.

## 6. What holds up

- **The pilot design:** testing the exact pattern before bidding is better evidence than most growth bids offer.
- **Sunday demand:** strong, close to weekday daytime levels.
- **The staffing arithmetic** and the two-staff assumption, which follows Council policy.
- **The survey evidence:** 44% of working-age non-users cite opening hours. That is a reasonable indicator of need, though stated barriers tend to overstate what people will actually do.
- **Recruitment risk is low**, since existing staff covered the pilot.

## 7. What is settled and what is open

**Settled by the paper's own figures:**
- the cost lines total £164,000;
- evening use is about 40% of daytime use, not close to it;
- Sunday use matches daytime;
- the pilot ran six months.

**Open, and what would settle each question:**
- **The £10,000 gap.** Settled by finding the missing line or correcting the total.
- **Net additional visits at Ashgrove.** Settled by total visits over the pilot period against the same months a year earlier.
- **Demand at the other four branches.** Settled by projections from each branch's own visit rates, or a staged roll-out.
- **Summer demand.** Settled by Ashgrove usage data from April 2026 onward, if opening continued.
- **Self-service and hybrid options.** Settled by a three-to-five-year cost comparison.

## 8. Suggested revision to the conclusion

> A six-month pilot at Ashgrove, our busiest branch, found Sunday use at about the same rate as weekday daytime (52 visits an hour) and evening use at about 40% of it (21 an hour). New memberships rose by about two-thirds on the previous year. Extending the pattern to five branches would cost £164,000 a year [or £174,000 with the missing item identified]. At Ashgrove rates this would give up to 84,000 visits in the new hours; Sunday hours cost about £1 per visit in staffing and evening hours about £2.40. We ask Members to approve the extension, with a review at six months against stated usage thresholds, and to note the option of a Sunday-led pattern if evening use at other branches is lower.

I can rebuild the cost table to show evening and Sunday costs separately, with a branch-by-branch visit estimate, if that would help.
